c11_acc_cbse_07_007: Crediting depreciation to the asset isn't money coming in — it's allocating past cost. The credit goes to Depreciation, never to Bank.
c12_acc_cbse_07_008: Managerial remuneration sits inside Employee Benefits Expense on the P&L face — its break-up belongs in the Notes. And 5% per MD vs 11% overall are different limits.
c11_acc_cbse_07_008: Under the provision method the asset stays at original cost — credit Provision for Depreciation, not the asset. On sale, move the accumulated provision across first.
c12_acc_cbse_07_009: Accumulated depreciation is a contra-asset netted off the gross block, not a liability. Provision for doubtful debts is a charge; reserve is an appropriation.
c11_acc_cbse_07_009: A provision is a charge against profit (made even in loss years); a reserve is an appropriation of profit. Credit balance alone doesn't make it a reserve.
c12_acc_cbse_07_010: Every adjustment hits twice — once in P&L, once in the Balance Sheet. Outstanding salary raises the expense and creates a liability. Check both effects.
c11_acc_cbse_07_010: A reserve fund is just an appropriation entry — no cash moves to a separate account until the firm decides to invest it. Check whether money actually moved.
c12_acc_cbse_07_011: The Balance Sheet face stays condensed under Schedule III — outstanding and prepaid items go inside the main heads, with break-ups in the Notes to Accounts.
c11_acc_cbse_07_011: Provision for depreciation is a charge spreading the asset's cost — not a reserve keeping profit aside for replacement. Check the purpose: matching vs retaining.
c12_acc_cbse_08_001: A ratio is a whistle-blower, not the answer — compare it to industry and past years and link it to a decision before concluding anything.
c11_acc_cbse_07_012: A secret reserve comes from deliberate under-statement (excess provision, capital spend expensed) — land appreciating to ₹50 lakh is just an unrealised gain.
c12_acc_cbse_08_002: Keep the two lists separate: data limits (historical cost, inflation, policies) hit all analysis; ratio limits (no benchmark, indicative only) are specific to ratios.
c11_acc_cbse_08_001: Ask whether the spend brings future benefit, not whether the amount is big or the asset new — a life-extending overhaul is capital; big advance rent isn't.
c12_acc_cbse_08_003: Comparative statements are the tool, horizontal analysis is the act — if you haven't computed absolute and % change, you've made a statement, not analysed.
c11_acc_cbse_08_002: Factory location doesn't make a cost direct — supervisor salary and factory insurance are indirect. Ask: was it incurred to bring goods to saleable condition?
c12_acc_cbse_08_004: Percentage change uses the previous year as base — it measures growth from then. And decreases need brackets or a minus sign; a zero base means 'not comparable'.
c11_acc_cbse_08_003: Split it: production wages go to the Trading Account, office salaries to P&L. If the figure is combined without factory detail, it sits in P&L.
c12_acc_cbse_08_005: Percentages alone can mislead — a small % rise on a big expense base can outweigh a big % rise on revenue. Check the absolute change and the margin.
c11_acc_cbse_08_004: Direct expenses like factory rent and carriage inwards belong in the Trading Account — don't dump every Trial Balance expense into P&L. Check the expense's nature.
c12_acc_cbse_08_006: In a common-size Balance Sheet, both sides use the grand total (assets = liabilities + equity) as the base — and write percentages with the % sign.
c11_acc_cbse_08_005: Direct expenses already used in the Trading Account mustn't re-enter P&L — wages there would double-count and understate net profit. Follow the two-stage split.
c12_acc_cbse_08_007: In a common-size P&L, every item is a share of Revenue from Operations — not of total expenses. Same logic as the Balance Sheet using its own grand total.
c11_acc_cbse_08_006: Closing stock isn't in the Trial Balance — it enters through the adjustment entry (Dr Closing Stock, Cr Trading). A 'Stock' figure there is usually opening stock.
c12_acc_cbse_08_008: Pick a normal year as base — one free of strikes or one-off gains — and trend % is current ÷ base × 100, so the base year itself reads 100.
c11_acc_cbse_08_007: Fixed vs current isn't about physical form — goodwill and patents are non-current, prepaid expenses can be current. Check the operating cycle and purpose.
c12_acc_cbse_08_009: Internal vs external isn't just who asks — it's the question and the data: internal uses transaction-level detail to fix operations; external uses aggregates to judge capital.
c11_acc_cbse_08_008: Not every bank loan is non-current — working-capital loans and the portion of long-term debt due within 12 months are current. Check the repayment schedule.
c12_acc_cbse_09_001: The cash flow statement isn't the cash book or profit — and under AS-3, interest paid by a non-financial company is financing, not operating. Check the firm's type.
